body_markdown:
I only get to fix cars and motorcycles. And by “fix,” I mean “take parts and pieces dreamt up by one person and produced by someone else, and piece them together after years of abuse (probably suffered at my own hands, because I probably stored the parts on a cracked concrete floor) while overthinking almost every detail of the process.” Like most of us, I don’t get to *build* cars or motorcycles. I can assemble them, I can modify them if I’m feeling particularly motivated, and, of course, I can enjoy driving them, but I can’t experience the satisfaction of starting with raw materials and creating something new and useful. Well, unless I want to build something with four wheels and no engine, which is exactly what I did last weekend.


Longtime readers will know that I am a proponent of working *on* your[shop or garage](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/the-real-project-that-never-ends-your-garage/) in addition to working *in* the garage. Taking a small amount of time to make the space more functional, organized, or inviting can make a successful project more triumphant and a frustrating one more tolerable. Simply the idea of a clear workbench is enough to get some people excited about working on a project, so imagine the dopamine hit to my brain when I came up with the idea to build a *new* workbench.


Is 2.5″ tubing with 1/4″ wall thickness too much? Probably. It’s also perfect.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


I love my extended Chevrolet Express van for a lot of reasons, and fitting 12-foot sticks of material with the doors closed is towards the top of the list.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Using three jack stands creates one plane and keeps things as flat as I can.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


My garage is well-equipped these days. I’ve been able to accumulate almost all of the large items needed to disassemble, clean, and rebuild (with relative efficiency) the cars, trucks, and motorcycles I enjoy playing with. A few of the larger projects require trips to better-equipped facilities owned by my friends, but at this point I’ve accepted that there will always be bigger fish. That said, I was getting quite tired of making a trip across town to use a parts washer. In a recent bout of horse trading, I brought home an empty parts-washer tub, a steel cabinet, and a bunch of steel tubing. I think everyone can guess where this is going.


For once, I spent a long weekend in the garage building something—[not rebuilding](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/your-project-car-doesnt-care-if-youre-an-expert/) , cleaning, or diagnosing something, or even reassembling someone else’s vision in a novel way, but taking an idea and making it reality. Are the results good? Well, kind of. There is a twist in the base that makes the whole bench tripod in certain spots on the uneven floor of my garage—and that’s after I cut apart my first attempt and re-welded everything with less twist. Uneven floors serve to remind me that triangles really are the super shape and can help make things flat and level.


A little cleanup and paint make even my welds look presentable.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The footprint is not large, and the top was yet to be trimmed, but seeing it shape up was nice.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


This parts washer had flimsy legs. I opted to build it into the workbench with more sturdy attachment points.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Now I only need to make the brackets to hold the parts washer in place.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


That’s all you’ll hear from me about[fabrication tips](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/7-fabrication-tools-that-belong-in-your-garage/) , because I am neither a fabricator nor a welder. I own a welder, but that does not make me a welder. If that line of thinking held true, my piston-ring compressor would make me an engine builder, and my air compressor and HVLP spray gun would magically make me a painter. Hardly. My ability to do an okay job once does not make me an expert. Some years ago I was traveling with a friend at a car event, and he showed someone an image he had taken at a previous event. “Wow, you must have a really nice camera,” they said. He didn’t. He spent the time learning how to use what he had to get the results he wanted. He wasn’t any more of a photographer than I am a welder. The results can be better than the tools on hand if care and attention is given.


Still, my new workbench is not a piece of art that will be appreciated by future generations for its elegance and durability. It is simply a highly functional addition to my garage, providing more drawers to organize tools, more worktop space to collect things that need attention, and a parts washer that I really have been needing for a few years. A partially complete parts washer, anyway. For now, it is just a tub as I finalize my plan for making it functional before I dig into the handful of engines that need attention this winter.


Even though I got multiple parts of this bench for free, this was not a financially smart endeavor. The steel was an okay deal considering I don’t have a connection. The butcher-block top I bought full price from a home center, and the double-locking casters I purchased new as well. The total is a little over $700, but this is built sturdier than the other benches in my shop, which have survived over 10 years of abuse without any type of meaningful wear. I choose to call that $700 an investment. The four days spent building it were an investment also, because focusing on the garage has supercharged the projects I have planned for this winter.


More than anything, building this bench was an exercise in stretching my brain. I set out to build something with an idea in my head but without a manual, drawing, or real plan, and I’m pretty happy with the result. Building something to our own specifications, when we are used to restoring or riffing on things others have built to their own specifications, was an interesting challenge—and one I think I only need to take on every once in a while.


The drawers fit a bunch of tools that had been overflowing my shelves for a bit.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


This doesn’t have a pump or solvent yet, but for now, simply having a designated dirty space is nice.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The narrow cabinet still leaves enough room to hold my jack stands and travel torch setup.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


These gas cans were constantly getting in the way; now they have a nice ledge to live on.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


It’s not going to win any beauty contests, but it was fun to build and will be even more fun to use for years.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)
